Biography: Hannah Darabi, born in 1981 in Tehran, Iran. Benoît Grimbert, born in 1969 in Mantes-la-Jolie, France. They live and work in Paris, France. The duo followed and photographed six students in their habits and practices, thereby creating a series of portraits of territories. The specific territory they inhabit, travel through, or cross itself constitutes a major element of the subject, allowing perspectives on Greater Paris to be both those of the artists and those of its inhabitants.

Kubra Khademi (born 1989) is an Afghan performance artist based in Paris. She studied fine arts at Kabul University before attending Beaconhouse National University in Lahore, Pakistan on a scholarship. In Lahore she began to create public performances, a practice she continued upon her return to Kabul, where her work actively responded to a society dominated by extreme patriarchal politics. After performing her piece Armor in 2015, Khademi was forced to flee Afghanistan due to a fatwa and death threats. She is currently living and working in Paris.

Baya Mahieddine or Fatima Haddad was an Algerian artist. While she did not identify her work as belonging to a particular art genre, critics have classified her paintings as surrealist, primitive, naïve, and modern. She was an entirely self-taught artist, working both as a painter and, to a lesser extent, in pottery. At the age of sixteen Baya had her first exhibition, in Paris, where she gained notice from artists such as Pablo Picasso and André Breton. Her work was presented in various exhibitions in France and Algeria, and has appeared on Algerian postage stamps.

Nadia Benbouta is an Algerian artist who lives and works in Paris. She uses photographs and images from her travels, combining them with cultural and decorative motifs to create contrast within her visuals. Born in Algiers, she received education at two art schools, the École supérieure des beaux-arts d'Alger and the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts. Her art combines unassuming elements like found images from advertisements, children's films, comic artwork, and decorative designs. She pairs these innocuous visuals with militaristic imagery and weaponry, creating disparity within the image. Her work has a tragic, cynical view of the world, using dark imagery to explore it. Benbouta works across many visual mediums. Her body of work includes photography, painting, printmaking, street art, neon lights, etc. Her work has been displayed in solo shows in France, Germany and the Ukraine. She has participated in group exhibitions in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Toulouse, Germany, Norway, Greece, Algeria and New York City. Benbouta received the Prix L`Art et la route, her first award, in 1997.  She also received the Prix Albéric Rocheron in 1998 and the Prix Fenêtre des Arts Européens awarded by the Sprengel Museum in Hanover in 1999. Her work is held in the collections of the Bibliothèque nationale de France, the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts, the Musée de Serignan and the town of Bobigny.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Aubervilliers (Seine-Saint-Denis, France) and in Casablanca (Morocco)
Biography: Zoulikha Bouabdellah (born 20 June 1977) is a Russian-born contemporary artist of Algerian descent. She lives and works in Casablanca and Paris. The daughter of Hassen Bouabdellah, a film director and author, and Malika Dorbani, former head of the National Museum of Fine Arts of Algiers, she was born on 20 June 1977 in Moscow and grew up in Algiers. Bouabdellah moved to France in 1993 during the Algerian Civil War. Her work explores the blending of cultures and globalization, religion, language, and intimacy as well as the female condition. It incorporates sculpture, photography, video and drawing, and she often contrasts traditional trappings of religion, e.g. prayer rugs, with symbols of modernity.

Born in Buenos Aires in 1950, Maria Amaral draws from her experience of exile, her Latin American roots, and her love of humanity the strength behind a vibrant and uncompromising art. Trained at the School of Fine Arts in Paris and inspired by Käthe Kollwitz, Guayasamín, and Van Gogh, she paints the human soul with passion, sensitivity, and power. Her father, a pastor, and her mother, a schoolteacher—both exiles from Spain—found refuge in Argentina in 1949 after years of resistance. It was there, in Buenos Aires, on December 25, 1950, that Maria Amaral was born. In 1967, she too experienced exile when she left with her entire family. France welcomed them, and it was first in Strasbourg and later at the Paris School of Fine Arts, where she earned the Advanced Diploma in Visual Arts, that her destiny as an artist truly took shape.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Périgny (Val-de-Marne, France)
Biography: Alicia Zadan was born in 1942 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and lives in Val-de-Marne, France. Since 1996, her sole subject has been the tree. Rounded trees, flame-like trees, cactus-like trees with bare, threatening branches. Trees of the city and trees of the countryside. The former are rendered in graphite, suffocated within a hostile, cubic, and geometricized environment. The latter, painted in gouache and acrylic, stand isolated in an orchard, often accompanied by a ladder. The diversity of her imaginary species and the variety of their presentations bring her work to the threshold of pure painting—painting for its own sake.

Mark Brusse is a Dutch painter and sculptor born on July 25, 1937, in Alkmaar, the Netherlands, who has lived and worked in Paris for most of his career. After studying at the Academy of Fine Arts in Arnhem in 1959, he received a scholarship to spend eight months in Paris, where he settled and created his first wooden assemblages. In 1961, he held his first solo exhibition in Paris and began developing his renowned series Clôtures, Soft Machines, and Strange Fruits, using reclaimed wood and found metal objects collected from the streets. These assemblages brought together chance discoveries, transforming them into poetic compositions with new meanings and stories. During this period, Brusse associated with artists of the Nouveau Réalisme movement and maintained close friendships with Robert Filliou and Daniel Spoerri. In 1967, he worked in New York, and the following year he held a solo exhibition at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam while reconnecting with the Fluxus movement. His collaborations with composer John Cage and participation in numerous happenings deepened his interest in environmental and site-specific installations. After spending time in Berlin in the early 1970s, he returned to Paris and settled at La Ruche, the historic artists` residence, where he continued creating assemblages from a wide variety of materials. His international reputation grew through major exhibitions, including the 1975 Venice Biennale, exhibitions at the Musée d`Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, and monumental sculpture projects in South Korea. Alongside sculpture and assemblage, painting regained an important place in his later work, and in 2008 he produced a print for a special art portfolio associated with the prestigious Jacques Goddet Prize. Marta Minujín was born in the San Telmo neighborhood of Buenos Aires. Her father was a Jewish physician and her mother a housewife of Spanish descent. She met a young economist, Juan Carlos Gómez Sabaini, and married him in secret in 1959; the couple had two children. As a student in the National University Art Institute, she first exhibited her work in a 1959 show at the Teatro Agón. A scholarship from the National Arts Foundation allowed her to travel to Paris as one of the young Argentina artists featured in Pablo Curatella Manes and Thirty Argentines of the New Generation, a 1960 exhibit organized by the prominent sculptor and Paris Biennale judge.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom)
Biography: Amalia Pica (born 1978 in Neuquén, Argentina) is a London-based Argentine artist who explores metaphor, communication, and civic participation through sculptures, installations, photographs, projections, live performances, and drawings. Pica was born in the late 1970s during the Dirty War, a period of state terrorism in Argentina. In light of this fact, Pica's work raises questions about the role of government, language and communication, and human connections. Much of her work explores fundamental issues of communication, such as the acts of delivering and receiving messages (verbal or nonverbal) and the various forms these exchanges may take. Victor Grippo, Cildo Meireles, Lygia Clark and Hélio Oiticica, among others, were the artists that Pica first studied.

Born in Argentina, Ana Axpe moved to Geneva in 1990, where she pursued artistic studies at the Higher School of Visual Arts (now HEAD), graduating in 1999. From the mid-1990s onward, she gained recognition for her video works, often based on documents related to the Spanish Civil War or the Argentine dictatorship, intertwined with personal memories that she usually narrates herself through voice-over. These videos were inspired by her father, a politically engaged Basque who had emigrated to Argentina. She subsequently developed a body of work focused on the human body, which she “fragmented” into isolated parts shown in close-up, while also exploring themes of split identity and stereotypical representations of women—subjects closely connected to her mother`s mental illness. In 1996, Axpe began ¡No Firmo!, a long-term artistic project. Conceived as a fictional telenovela (the Latin American equivalent of a soap opera), it centers on the character Adela Conti, played by Ana Axpe, who assumes the identity of her sister Olga, also portrayed by the artist. Olga has gone mad and been institutionalized, while Adela lives out her sister’s glamorous, artistic, and highly caricatured existence. Through this work, Axpe satirizes both the aesthetic conventions of telenovelas and contemporary celebrity culture, weaving a disorienting narrative that blurs the boundaries between reality and fiction. In her exhibitions, she expands the twelve-episode series with posters, “documentary” films, photographs, and personal objects belonging to Adela. This subversive role-playing forms an essential part of Ana Axpe’s broader reflection on personal and social realities.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Buenos Aires (Argentina)
Biography: Ana Gallardo is a visual artist, feminist activist, weaver of bonds that are part of her life and her work. She works with the languages within her reach, she is self-taught and autobiographical. Her mother was an artist and died when she was very young; like her mother, she began painting, but realized, as time went by, that she was terrible at it. After several unsuccessful attempts to be recognized for her work, after sending her pieces to different contests, and trying to insert herself in a market designed mainly for men, she decided to close her workshop. Tidying up her things, in her eagerness to put an end to a phase, she taped each of her tools to the wall. When a friend arrived at the house and saw what she had done, he thought that there was a new work. In the eye that observed and in Ana herself a mean was born, which was pictorial but also sculptural, in which a new way of producing found its form.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Bucks (United Kingdom) since 1969
Biography: Carmen Gracia RE (born 1935) is an Argentine artist-printmaker. Gracia left Argentina for Paris in 1960 and joined the printmaking studio Atelier 17, run by William Hayter. She later studied at the Slade School of Fine Art. Examples of Gracia's work are included in the British Council art collection, the UK Government Art Collection, the Victoria and Albert Museum the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, the Cuming Museum, the Indianapolis Museum of Art and the Chazen Museum of Art.

Irene Kopelman (born 1974, Córdoba, Argentina) is an Argentine-Dutch artist based in Amsterdam. Her works explore the relationship between science and art. Kopelman's work marries the clinical distance of scientific observation with an almost spiritual reverence for landscape and the objects, large and small, that comprise it. It is built on the long-term engagement with ecological issues and the parallels between both science and art. The subject matter is a close visual engagement, questioning and exploring how drawing can approach these topics. Her work forms knowledge through the image and the process to make the image about the environment. They also embody the methodologies and systems we use to generate the knowledge and make it visible, creating her own systems of representation through artworks.

Mirtha Dermisache was an Argentine artist whose works of asemic writing have been published and exhibited internationally at venues including the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris and MACBA in Barcelona, and collected by leading international arts institutions. She won the Konex Award in 2012 (posthumous) in Concept Art.

Leonor Fini was an Argentine-Italian painter, illustrator, designer, writer, and one of the most distinctive figures associated with Surrealism. Born in Buenos Aires, she was raised in Trieste after her mother fled an oppressive marriage, and her unconventional childhood, marked by family conflicts and frequent disguises to avoid custody disputes, deeply influenced her imagination. Largely self-taught, Fini developed her artistic vision through exposure to the Renaissance and Mannerist traditions of Italy rather than formal academic training. After early success in Milan, she settled in Paris in 1931, where she became part of an influential artistic circle that included Max Ernst, Salvador Dalí, Pablo Picasso, Paul Éluard, and Giorgio de Chirico. Although she never officially joined the Surrealist movement, she exhibited alongside its members and became one of its most original female voices. Her paintings are renowned for their depictions of powerful, sensual, and enigmatic women, as well as recurring motifs such as sphinxes, witches, and androgynous figures. Beyond painting, Fini enjoyed a prolific career as a costume and set designer for theatre, ballet, opera, and film, collaborating with major cultural figures including Roland Petit and Benjamin Britten. She also designed the iconic bottle for Elsa Schiaparelli`s perfume *Shocking* and illustrated around fifty books, including works by Charles Baudelaire, Edgar Allan Poe, Jean Genet, and the celebrated erotic novel *Histoire d’O*. Throughout her life, Fini maintained close friendships with leading writers, artists, and intellectuals, while her portraits captured many of the cultural personalities of twentieth-century Paris. Her multidisciplinary career, spanning painting, illustration, literature, and stage design, established her as one of the most innovative and independent women artists of the twentieth century.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New York (New York, United States)
Biography: Liliana Porter (born 1941) is an Argentine contemporary artist whose multidisciplinary practice encompasses photography, printmaking, painting, drawing, installation, video, theater, and public art. Born in Buenos Aires, she spent part of her youth in Mexico City, where she studied with influential artists Guillermo Silva Santamaria and Mathias Goeritz before completing her education at the National School of Fine Arts in Buenos Aires. In 1964, she moved to New York City, a decisive step that established her international artistic career and connected her with the vibrant contemporary art scene of the United States. That same year, she co-founded the New York Graphic Workshop alongside Luis Camnitzer and José Guillermo Castillo, contributing significantly to the development of conceptual printmaking practices. Throughout her career, Porter has explored themes of memory, identity, time, fiction, and the relationship between reality and representation. Her work is particularly known for incorporating miniature figures, found objects, and carefully staged scenes that blur the boundaries between the everyday and the imaginary. In addition to her artistic production, she has played an important role as an educator, teaching at several institutions and helping to shape new generations of artists. In 1974, she co-founded Studio Camnitzer in Italy, an international residency program that welcomed artists working across diverse media. From 1991 to 2007, she served as a professor at Queens College of the City University of New York, further strengthening her influence within the academic and artistic communities. Today, Porter is recognized as one of the leading Latin American contemporary artists, celebrated for her innovative and poetic works that challenge conventional perceptions of narrative, space, and human experience.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Buenos Aires (Argentina) and in New York (New York, United States)
Biography: Magdalena Jitrik (born 1966 in Buenos Aires, Argentina) is a contemporary Argentine artist whose work explores the intersections of art, politics, history, and collective memory. She spent part of her childhood and youth in Mexico, where she began her artistic education at the National School of Visual Arts before returning to Argentina. Since her first solo exhibition in 1990, Jitrik has developed a distinctive practice centered on revolutionary utopias, leftist political traditions, and the relationship between artistic expression and social transformation. Her paintings draw on abstraction and modernist formal languages while incorporating references to historical uprisings, political slogans, and acts of resistance. Through series such as *Manifesto*, *Revolts*, and *Disobedience*, she seeks to expand painting beyond aesthetics into a space of historical and political reflection. Between 2002 and 2007, she was a founding member of the Taller Popular de Serigrafía, a collective that emerged from the social movements following Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis and became known for its public interventions and activist printmaking. Her engagement with grassroots organizations and community initiatives has included collaborations with neighborhood assemblies and memorial projects addressing state violence and historical trauma. Throughout her career, Jitrik has examined events and figures such as the Paris Commune, the Black Panther movement, and the Auschwitz Sonderkommando, investigating the power and limits of visual representation in confronting injustice and collective memory. Her work has been presented at major international biennials, including Porto Alegre, Thessaloniki, Istanbul, and Manifesta, and she has also developed curatorial projects and research focused on socialist and libertarian imaginaries. Today, her works are held in leading public and private collections, including the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid, MACBA in Barcelona, MALBA in Buenos Aires, and the Museo Universitario de Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City, confirming her position as one of the most significant voices in contemporary Latin American art.

Nina Negri (1901–1981) was an Argentine-French painter and engraver associated with Surrealism and renowned for her pioneering contributions to experimental printmaking. Born in Rosario, Argentina, she began her artistic education in Buenos Aires before continuing her studies in Oxford, Belgium, and France, later complementing her artistic training with studies in psychology and Native American anthropology. By 1921, she had settled in Paris, where she studied under influential artists André Lhote, Fernand Léger, and Marcel Gromaire. Through her teachers, she was introduced to the celebrated printmaker Stanley William Hayter and became an active member of Atelier 17, one of the most innovative printmaking studios of the twentieth century. Throughout the 1930s, Negri participated in major Parisian exhibitions, including the Salon des Indépendants and the Salon de Mai, while developing experimental engraving techniques alongside other Atelier 17 artists. She was among the first artists to explore new methods of color printing, helping to pioneer approaches that later became known as simultaneous color printmaking. In 1938, her work was included in the landmark International Surrealist Exhibition, where she stood out as one of the few artists exhibiting engravings. Her international reputation continued to grow through exhibitions in Europe and the Americas, including participation in the influential 1944 exhibition *Hayter and Studio 17: New Directions in Gravure* at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. After World War II, she increasingly embraced abstraction, combining technical innovation with a highly personal visual language. Returning to Atelier 17 in Paris in the 1950s, she continued her experiments with color printing and relief engraving, establishing herself as an important figure in the history of modern printmaking and abstract art.

Alicia Penalba (1913–1982) was an Argentine sculptor, tapestry designer, and weaver whose innovative abstract sculptures established her as one of the leading figures of postwar modern sculpture. Born in San Pedro, Buenos Aires Province, she initially pursued drawing and painting before dedicating herself entirely to sculpture after settling in Paris in 1950. Influenced by artists such as Étienne Martin and Étienne Hajdu, she developed a distinctive visual language based on organic, non-figurative forms that contributed to the renewal of abstract sculpture in the mid-twentieth century. Her early works were characterized by dynamic vertical structures that evoked natural growth, movement, and spiritual energy. During the 1960s, her artistic approach evolved toward broader and more horizontal compositions while maintaining her commitment to abstraction. Penalba became particularly renowned for her monumental sculptures, many of which were installed in public spaces and museum collections around the world. Among her most celebrated works is *The Great Double* (*Le Grand Double*), a monumental sculpture displayed at the Kröller-Müller Museum in the Netherlands and in Milwaukee, United States. Her international reputation was confirmed in 1961 when she received the International Sculpture Prize at the Fifth São Paulo Biennial, one of the most prestigious awards in contemporary art. Throughout her career, her work was exhibited widely and entered major collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago, the Kröller-Müller Museum, the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, and the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes in Buenos Aires. Today, Alicia Penalba is recognized as a pioneering figure in abstract sculpture whose powerful organic forms continue to influence generations of artists and whose legacy was further celebrated through her inclusion in the landmark exhibition *Women in Abstraction* at the Centre Pompidou in 2021.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Buenos Aires (Argentina)
Biography: Marina De Caro (born 1961 in Mar del Plata, Argentina) is a contemporary multidisciplinary artist who lives and works in Buenos Aires and is known for her exploration of space, the body, emotion, and sensory experience. Her artistic practice encompasses drawing, installation, sculpture, textiles, performance, and spatial interventions, creating immersive environments that engage both the physical and emotional presence of the viewer. For De Caro, drawing represents the essential starting point of every project, serving as a means of expressing forms that emerge from intuition, memory, and the imagination. Her works are characterized by vibrant colors and fantastical, baroque, and dreamlike imagery that blur the boundaries between reality and fiction. Central to her practice is the body, which she considers both a subject and a medium through which space can be experienced and transformed. Through installations and performances, she creates poetic environments where movement, gesture, and narrative unfold in dialogue with architectural space. De Caro frequently incorporates handcrafted textiles, garments, and woven structures that function simultaneously as sculptural objects and performative elements. Her works invite viewers to engage not only visually but also physically and emotionally, emphasizing the relationship between the body and its surroundings. By combining drawing, sculpture, performance, and textile art, she constructs open-ended worlds where imagination and sensory perception take precedence over fixed meanings. Today, Marina De Caro is recognized as one of Argentina’s leading contemporary artists, celebrated for her innovative fusion of visual art, performance, and spatial experimentation.

Graciela Sacco (1956–2017) was an influential Argentine artist born in Chañar Ladeado and based in Rosario, whose multidisciplinary practice combined photography, painting, installation, and video to examine the complex relationship between art and everyday life. Deeply inspired by the politically engaged artistic actions of *Tucumán Arde* (Tucumán Is Burning), organized by the Grupo de Artistas de Vanguardia in Rosario in 1968, she developed a body of work that challenged traditional exhibition formats and sought direct engagement with public space. Rather than confining art to galleries and museums, Sacco brought her projects into urban environments, creating what she described as “urban interferences” that disrupted routine perceptions and encouraged critical reflection on social, political, and cultural realities. Through powerful visual interventions addressing themes such as migration, exclusion, memory, violence, and collective experience, she established herself as one of the most significant voices in contemporary Latin American art.
Judi Werthein was born in 1967 in Buenos Aires. She lives and works in Brooklyn and Buenos Aires. Leandro Erlich was born in 1973 in Buenos Aires. He lives and works in Argentina and Paris.

Biography: Christian Liberté Boltanski (6 September 1944 – 14 July 2021) was a French sculptor, photographer, painter, and film maker. He is best known for his photography installations and contemporary French conceptual style. Mauricio Pezo (b. Renaico, Chile, 1973) is an artist, architect and educator. In 2002, together with Sofia von Ellrichshausen, he found the art and architecture studio Pezo von Ellrichshausen. They live and work in southern Chile, in a farm at the foot of the Andes Mountains. Sofía von Ellrichshausen (born 1976) is an Argentine-Chilean architect, artist, and educator. In 2002, she co-founded the art and architecture studio «Pezo von Ellrichshausen» in Concepción, Chile, together with Mauricio Pezo. Their work has been exhibited at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, and the Venice Biennale of Architecture, and is part of the permanent collections of the Art Institute of Chicago and the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Novera Ahmed (1939–2015) was a pioneering Bangladeshi modernist sculptor widely regarded as one of the founders of modern sculpture in Bangladesh. Born in the Sundarbans during British India and raised in a family with strong artistic influences, she developed an early fascination with three-dimensional forms through her mother’s traditional clay modeling. She studied in Calcutta and Comilla before moving to London, where she earned a diploma in design, modeling, and sculpture from Camberwell College of Arts and trained under prominent European artists including Jacob Epstein and Karel Vogel. Her artistic development continued in Florence and Vienna, where she was exposed to European modernist sculpture and influenced by masters such as Henry Moore. Returning to what is now Bangladesh, Ahmed collaborated with architect Hamidur Rahman on the original design of the iconic Shaheed Minar in Dhaka, a national symbol of the Language Movement. Between 1956 and 1960, she produced around one hundred sculptures, introducing a bold modernist visual language that was unprecedented in the region. In 1957, she created the first sculptural frieze for the Dhaka Central Public Library, marking an important milestone in the history of public art in Bangladesh. Her works were exhibited in Dhaka, Lahore, and later Paris, where her final exhibition took place in 1973, while many of her sculptures are now preserved in the Bangladesh National Museum. Despite being ahead of her time and often underappreciated during her career, her innovative approach profoundly influenced subsequent generations of South Asian artists. In recognition of her outstanding contribution to art and culture, she received the Ekushey Padak in 1997 and was posthumously awarded the Independence Award in 2025, cementing her legacy as one of Bangladesh’s most important modern artists.

Kenia Almaraz Murillo is a Bolivian-born contemporary textile artist whose work explores themes of memory, migration, ancestry, and diasporic identity through large-scale woven installations. Born in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia, she moved to Paris at the age of eleven, separated from her parents, and gradually adapted to a new culture while maintaining a strong connection to her Andean heritage. A transformative return visit to Bolivia during her adolescence reawakened vivid childhood memories and deepened her appreciation for the *aguayos*—traditional woven textiles preserved by her family as treasured heirlooms. Discovering that both her grandmother and great-grandmother were accomplished weavers, Almaraz Murillo came to view these textiles as living archives that carry the traces of generations of women in her family. Inspired by this legacy, she brought the *aguayos* back to France and incorporated their cultural significance into her artistic practice. Trained in weaving in Paris by the renowned textile artist Simone Prouvé, she developed a distinctive visual language that merges traditional Andean textile techniques with contemporary artistic expression. Her monumental wall-based sculptures are handwoven using indigenous South American fibers and enriched with found urban materials such as vehicle reflectors, motorcycle headlights, and objects sourced from Bolivian markets. By combining these elements with neon lighting, embroidery, and references to modern urban life, she creates works that bridge past and present, tradition and modernity. Recent projects draw inspiration from the costumes and symbolism of the famous Carnival of Oruro, where pre-Columbian Andean deities coexist with Catholic traditions, reflecting Bolivia’s complex cultural history and resilience. Through her vibrant and immersive textile installations, Almaraz Murillo offers a powerful reflection on cultural transmission, collective memory, and the experience of belonging between multiple worlds.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina) and in Düsseldorf (Germany)
Biography: Danica Dakić (born 1962 in Sarajevo) is a Bosnian contemporary artist, educator, and filmmaker whose multidisciplinary practice encompasses video, photography, installation, performance, sound, and sculpture. Raised in former Yugoslavia, she studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Sarajevo, completed a master’s degree in painting at the University of Arts in Belgrade, and later continued her artistic education at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf under the influential media artist Nam June Paik. Since moving to Germany in 1988, Dakić has developed an internationally acclaimed career while maintaining strong ties to Sarajevo, a city that remains central to her artistic vision. The experience of the Bosnian War and the Siege of Sarajevo profoundly shaped her work, leading her to explore themes of memory, displacement, identity, language, and the reconstruction of social and cultural narratives after conflict. Through extensive research and close collaboration with participants, she creates immersive projects that combine personal stories with broader historical and political contexts. Her works often transform architectural spaces, historical sites, and symbolic images into stages where alternative voices and perspectives can emerge beyond conventional social and political classifications. Early projects such as *MADAME X* (1997) and *WITNESS* (1998) addressed the aftermath of war and the complexities of collective memory in post-war Bosnia and Herzegovina. Working closely with long-term collaborators including photographer Egbert Trogemann, composer Bojan Vuletić, and producer Amra Bakšić Čamo, she develops ambitious interdisciplinary works that challenge established narratives and invite public participation. Her art has been exhibited internationally, including at Documenta 12 in Kassel and the 58th Venice Biennale, where she represented Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2019. Today, living and working between Düsseldorf, Weimar, and Sarajevo, Dakić is recognized as one of the most important contemporary artists from Southeast Europe, celebrated for her powerful exploration of identity, memory, and the social role of art.

Xenia, born in Sarajevo in 1928, was a distinguished sculptor whose career was shaped by both Balkan and French artistic traditions. After graduating from the Academy of Fine Arts in Belgrade, she refined her skills between 1956 and 1958 in the studio of Sreten Stojanović, a student of Antoine Bourdelle, and later continued her studies at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Yencesse, Zadkine, and Couturier. A member of the Circle of Friends of Bourdelle, she developed a sculptural language that placed her in the lineage of major twentieth-century sculptors such as Bourdelle and Giacometti. Working primarily in bronze, she focused on the human figure in motion, capturing not only physical movement but also the emotions and sensations experienced by the body. Her sculptures often evoke the grace of dancers, reflecting her fascination with gesture, balance, and the poetry of movement. Through a combination of technical mastery and sensitivity, she transformed fleeting moments into powerful artistic expressions imbued with elegance and humanity. Art critic Giulio-Enrico Pisani described her work, particularly the sculpture *Lilie*, as embodying a natural nobility and serenity, suggesting a vision akin to a Giacometti freed from anguish and turned toward tenderness. Her bronze figures reveal a humanity that is at once fragile and resilient, where vulnerability becomes a source of beauty and strength. Throughout her career, she received numerous awards and gained international recognition, with her works entering prestigious collections, including the Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris. Today, Xenia is remembered as a remarkable sculptor whose expressive and deeply human works continue to resonate with audiences worldwide.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography: Pamela Phatsimo Sunstrum is a visual artist. Her practice includes drawing, painting, installation, and animation. Her work has been featured in numerous exhibitions, including The Curve Space at The Barbican, The Hague, and the Centre for Fine Arts Bozar. Sunstrum was born in 1980 in Mochudi, Botswana, and spent her childhood in different parts of Africa and southeast Asia. She came to the United States in 1998 and received a BA with Highest Honors from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in International Studies with a concentration in Trans-national Cultures in 2004. Sunstrum received her MFA from the Mt. Royal School of Art at the Maryland Institute College of Art in 2007.She later lived in Baltimore Maryland as an artist in residence at the Baltimore Creative Alliance, while also teaching at the Maryland Institute College of Art. She is currently based out of Johannesburg, South Africa while showcasing in both individual and group exhibitions around the world. Sunstrum was appointed assistant professor in the Department of Visual Art & Art History of York University in 2017. After retiring from teaching in 2020, Sunstrum now lives and works in The Hague, The Netherlands. She is currently represented by Goodman Gallery and Galerie Lelong &Co. NYC. Sunstrum describes her work as her contribution to the rising tide of global voices dissenting against colonialism, apartheid, genocide, and all other forms of human and ecological oppression and exploitation that have spawned from centuries of capitalistic greed and corruption.

Maria Thereza Alves (born 1961 in São Paulo, Brazil) is a Brazilian-born artist, activist, writer, filmmaker, and researcher whose multidisciplinary practice examines the lasting effects of colonialism, migration, environmental change, and social injustice. As a child, she moved with her family to New York City to escape Brazil`s military dictatorship, an experience that deeply influenced her political and artistic outlook. She studied architecture at Cooper Union, graduating in 1985, and has since developed an internationally recognized career that combines artistic production with social and environmental activism. At the age of seventeen, she addressed the United Nations Human Rights Committee in Geneva on human rights violations against Indigenous peoples in Brazil, demonstrating an early commitment to political engagement. In 1987, she co-founded the Green Party of São Paulo, further strengthening her involvement in environmental and social causes. Her most celebrated long-term project, *Seeds of Change*, investigates the intertwined histories of colonial trade, slavery, migration, and global commerce through the study of plant seeds transported across continents in the ballast of colonial ships. Through research-based installations, videos, writings, and public interventions, Alves reveals hidden ecological and historical narratives that connect human and environmental histories. Her work has been presented at major international exhibitions, including Documenta 13, Manifesta 12, the Sharjah Biennial, and the Sydney Biennale, establishing her as an important voice in contemporary art. In 2016, she received the Vera List Center Prize for Art and Politics in recognition of her influential contributions to socially engaged artistic practice. Living and working in Berlin, Alves continues to create projects that challenge dominant historical narratives while advocating for environmental awareness, Indigenous rights, and social justice.

Birth / death: 1935, Rio de Janeiro (Brazil) - 2022, Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Sonia Andrade (born 1935 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is a pioneering Brazilian feminist artist and one of the founders of video art in Brazil, renowned for her politically charged works that challenge systems of power, media influence, and social control. Emerging during the military dictatorship of the 1970s, she was part of a generation of artists who responded to censorship and repression through experimental forms of personal and bodily expression. Studying under Anna Bella Geiger at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, Andrade developed a distinctive artistic language that combined performance, video, photography, installation, and sculpture. Her early video works often featured her own body subjected to uncomfortable and painful actions, such as wrapping her face with nylon thread, inserting nails between her fingers, or restricting movement with cages, creating powerful metaphors for political oppression and torture. Through these performances, she exposed the violence and psychological control embedded within authoritarian regimes while also questioning social conformity. Andrade was equally critical of mass media, particularly television, which she portrayed as a tool of manipulation and passive consumption. Works such as *Untitled* (1975) and *Untitled* (1977) used irony and repetition to challenge viewers` relationship with media and encourage critical awareness. Throughout her career, she expanded her practice to include drawing, photography, assemblage, neon works, sculpture, and large-scale installations, always emphasizing the relationship between the artwork and the spectator. Her celebrated series *Hydragrammas*, composed of hundreds of small assembled objects, exemplifies her interest in collective structures and visual complexity. Today, Sonia Andrade is recognized as a key figure in Latin American contemporary art whose groundbreaking use of video and performance continues to influence generations of artists and scholars.

Martha Araújo (born 1943 in Maceió, Brazil) is a Brazilian sculptor, performance artist, and educator whose work explores the relationship between the body, space, freedom, and repression. Emerging as an artist during the final years of Brazil’s military dictatorship (1964–1985), she developed a powerful artistic language that reflected the psychological and physical constraints experienced under authoritarian rule. Through sculpture, performance, photography, video, and textile-based works, Araújo investigates the limits of the human body and the tension between confinement and liberation. Her performances often use her own body as both subject and medium, transforming personal experience into a broader reflection on social and political realities. Textile structures play a central role in her practice, serving as metaphors for restriction, resistance, and the possibility of movement within imposed boundaries. Trained in education and pedagogy at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro and later at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, she combines intellectual inquiry with a deeply physical approach to art-making. Between 1984 and 1987, she worked under sculptor Haroldo Barroso at the Museu do Ingá in Niterói, further developing her sculptural practice. In 1986, she continued her artistic studies at the Escola de Artes Visuais do Parque Lage in Rio de Janeiro, one of Brazil’s most influential centers for contemporary art. Throughout her career, Araújo has challenged conventional distinctions between object, body, and action, creating works that require direct physical and emotional engagement from participants. Today, she is recognized as a significant figure in Brazilian contemporary art, celebrated for her innovative exploration of the body as a site of resistance, vulnerability, and transformation.

Frida Baranek (born 1961 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is a Brazilian sculptor renowned for her large-scale installations and sculptures that combine industrial materials with organic forms to explore the relationship between nature, technology, and contemporary society. Trained in architecture at Universidade Santa Úrsula in Rio de Janeiro and later in sculpture at Parsons School of Design in New York, she developed a distinctive artistic language that transforms steel, iron wire, metal plates, springs, glass, rubber, and other manufactured materials into dynamic, often biomorphic structures. Emerging as part of Brazil’s influential “Generation 80” movement, Baranek gained recognition for works that challenged traditional notions of sculpture by introducing unexpected poetic relationships between industrial objects and natural environments. Her sculptures frequently evoke nests, cocoons, constellations, fences, and organic growth, creating a visual tension between fragility and strength, order and chaos. Many of her works also contain subtle references to women’s experiences, incorporating woven threads, hair-like forms, and handcrafted techniques traditionally associated with feminine labor. Through the transformation of hard, industrial materials into delicate and sensuous compositions, she reflects on issues of industrialization, environmental change, and human interaction with the natural world. Her installations often occupy public spaces and landscapes, where they engage directly with architecture, water, and light. Having lived and worked in cities including Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paris, Berlin, New York, and Miami, Baranek has developed an international career while maintaining strong connections to Brazilian cultural and environmental concerns. Her works are included in major collections such as the Museum of Modern Art of São Paulo, the Museum of Contemporary Art of the University of São Paulo, the Kemper Art Museum, and the National Museum of Women in the Arts. Today, she is recognized as one of Brazil’s leading contemporary sculptors, celebrated for her ability to merge industrial materials with poetic and organic forms.

Elen Braga is a Brazilian artist living in Belgium. She’s a multidisciplinary visual artist in the fields of installation, sculpture, and public space. Her large-scale installations often accompany a performative aspect connected to the use of her own image. She challenges herself to work with new materials and techniques; sewing, ceramics, metal. Elen Braga researches themes such as strength-requiring and resilience. Her practice often involves self-imposed tasks, as well as intense labor-requiring endeavors. She delves into mythological narratives, revisiting them to examine the ways in which they survive in contemporary behavior and beliefs. Most of the time, her work is strongly concerned with the contexts of the places in which it is presented. At the same time, she plays with the paradoxes of materiality, trying to use different materials than those used in everyday life.

Sofia Caesar (1989, Brazil) is an artist, researcher, and choreographer. Her work investigates the apparatuses that document the moving and speaking body. Her recent projects reconstruct the making of documents (such as interviews and archival films) and the power relations that enable their functioning. She works across installation, video, and performance, generating speculative works in attempts to emancipate or undermine the authority of the documentation apparatus. She creates strategies to make the potentials for agency visible within processes that bind subjectivities to language, representation and/or documentation. Caesar has worked with institutions such as A Tale of a Tub, Rotterdam, NL; L’Iselp, Brussels; Parco d’Arte Vivente, Turin; La Maudite, Paris; SFMOMA, San Francisco; Tomie Othake Institute, São Paulo; A Gentil Carioca, Oi Futuro, Parque Lage, Capacete, Rio de Janeiro; and others. Her work Worker leaves the factory (conditions of work) is part of the permanent collection of Parco d'Arte Vivente (Living Art Museum) in Turin, Italy.

Lygia Pimentel Lins, better known as Lygia Clark, was a Brazilian artist best known for her painting and installation work. She was often associated with the Brazilian Constructivist movements of the mid-20th century and the Tropicalia movement. Along with Brazilian artists Amilcar de Castro, Franz Weissmann, Lygia Pape and poet Ferreira Gullar, Clark co-founded the Neo-Concrete movement. From 1960 on, Clark discovered ways for viewers (who would later be referred to as 'participants') to interact with her art works. Clark's work dealt with the relationship between inside and outside, and, ultimately, between self and world.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Rochelle Costi (1961-2022) was a Brazilian photographer, painter, and installation artist whose work offered a unique and insightful portrait of contemporary urban life in Brazil. Born in Caxias do Sul, she studied Social Communication at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul before establishing herself as one of the leading figures of Brazilian contemporary photography. After moving to São Paulo in 1988, she developed a distinctive artistic practice that combined photography, installation, and archival research to examine everyday environments and social behaviors. Her work often adopted a systematic and almost ethnographic approach, documenting domestic spaces, workplaces, public settings, and the habits of city dwellers in order to reveal the hidden structures of daily life. During the early 1990s, she expanded her artistic perspective while living in London, where she studied at Saint Martin`s School of Art and worked at the influential Camera Work gallery. Costi gained widespread recognition throughout the 1990s for projects that explored themes of consumption, memory, identity, and the organization of urban space. Her photographs are characterized by meticulous observation, humor, and a deep curiosity about the relationship between people and their surroundings. Over the course of her career, she participated in major international exhibitions and biennials, including the Havana Biennial, the Cuenca Biennial, and the São Paulo Biennial, while her works entered important museum collections across Europe, North and South America. Through her ability to transform ordinary scenes into compelling visual narratives, she created a valuable record of social and cultural life in contemporary Brazil. Today, Rochelle Costi is remembered as one of the most influential Brazilian artists of her generation, whose work continues to shape discussions about photography, urban experience, and visual culture.

Fabiana EX-SOUZA is an Afro-Brazilian artist and researcher, she explores colonial wounds through a transatlantic lens, developing a multidisciplinary practice that blends sculpture, performance, video, installation, and photography. Her work is deeply tied to self-invention and healing. Incorporating plant materials into her sculptures, she evokes rituals of transformation and repair. Her performances engage with the political dimension of art, tackling themes of hybridity, archival reactivation, transmission, and memory. By adopting the name “Ex-Souza,” she marks a rupture, re-signifying her family`s colonial legacy as a space of liberation. This perspective naturally led her to ecological care practices, which now play a central role in her artistic approach. A graduate of the École Guignard in Belo Horizonte (2010), Ex-Souza earned a Master of Arts from Université Paris 8 in 2012 and is currently completing a PhD in Visual Arts and Photography at the same institution. Her work has gained rapid recognition: in 2022, she was nominated for the Pernod Ricard Foundation Prize before winning the COAL Plante! Art and Environment Prize. In 2023, she was awarded the French Ministry of Culture`s Mondes Nouveaux grant and later received the SUITE/CNAP prize for 2024-2025. Her performances and installations have been showcased at major institutions and events, including the Dakar Biennale (2024), Lille Métropole Museum of Modern, Contemporary, and Outsider Art (2022), Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature (2023), Centre Pompidou (2016, 2019), Maison de l`Amérique Latine (2018), and Fondation Cartier (2015). Some of her works have recently entered public collections, including FRAC Nouvelle-Aquitaine and the Fonds d`Art Contemporain de la Ville de Paris.

Artist: Denise FERREIRA DA SILVA, Arjuna NEUMAN
Biography: Denise Ferreira da Silva (born 1963 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is a Brazilian philosopher, writer, artist, and activist whose work bridges critical theory, political thought, and contemporary artistic practice. Based in Vancouver, Canada, she is a professor at the University of British Columbia and director of the Institute for Gender, Race, Sexuality and Social Justice. Internationally recognized for her contributions to Black feminist theory, decolonial studies, and critiques of racial capitalism, she has authored influential books including Toward a Global Idea of Race (2007) and Unpayable Debt (2021). Extending her philosophical research beyond academia, Ferreira da Silva works across video, performance, poetry, installation, and collaborative projects that challenge conventional distinctions between theory and practice. Central to her artistic approach is the concept of “poethics,” which combines Black feminist thought, anti-colonial critique, and alternative forms of knowledge grounded in intuition, emotion, and relationality. Her work has been presented internationally at institutions and events including MACBA Barcelona, the Lubumbashi Biennial, and the 35th São Paulo Biennial. Through her interdisciplinary practice, she explores new ways of imagining social justice, collective transformation, and alternative futures beyond colonial and capitalist structures. Arjuna Neuman (born 1984 in the United Kingdom) is an artist, filmmaker, writer, and researcher whose work combines moving images, archival materials, digital technologies, sound, and experimental narrative structures. After studying Film and Video at the California Institute of the Arts, where he graduated in 2011, he developed a distinctive cinematic language that moves beyond conventional documentary formats to create immersive sensory experiences. His films blend original footage, historical archives, 3D animation, and drone imagery into layered visual compositions that explore questions of history, ecology, technology, and political power. Sound plays a central role in his work, weaving together interviews, ambient recordings, and music to create emotionally charged environments. Works such as First Fugue and Syncopated Green examine alternative histories and subcultures while challenging dominant cultural narratives. Since 2016, Neuman has collaborated extensively with Denise Ferreira da Silva on a series of films and installations they describe as “elemental cinema,” investigating the interconnected histories of colonialism, migration, extraction, and environmental transformation. His work has been exhibited internationally at major institutions and biennials, including the Sharjah Biennial, Berlin Biennale, Kunsthalle Wien, MACBA Barcelona, and the Ural Industrial Biennial. Through his innovative use of moving-image media, Neuman has established himself as an important voice in contemporary art, creating works that invite viewers to experience history and politics through sensation, imagination, and embodied perception.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Anna Bella Geiger (born 1933 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is one of the most influential figures in Brazilian contemporary art, renowned for her pioneering work across painting, printmaking, photography, video, installation, and conceptual art. Born to Polish-Jewish immigrant parents who settled in Brazil before her birth, Geiger initially studied literature and languages at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro before turning to visual arts in the 1950s under the guidance of artist Fayga Ostrower. She participated in her first exhibition at the age of seventeen and later expanded her artistic education in New York, where she studied art history at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Throughout her long career, Geiger has continually reinvented her practice, moving from abstraction to experimental forms that incorporate photomontage, photographic engraving, assemblage, sculpture, video, and cartographic imagery. During the 1970s, under the political climate of Brazil’s military dictatorship, she became a central figure in the development of conceptual art in Latin America, using maps, territories, and geographic symbols to question identity, power, and cultural belonging. Her works frequently explore themes of displacement, migration, memory, and the construction of national and personal narratives. In addition to her artistic production, Geiger has played a significant role as an educator, teaching at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, Columbia University, and the Escola de Artes Visuais do Parque Lage, where she influenced generations of artists. Her later projects combined installation, performance, video, and sculptural elements, exemplified by works such as *Circe*, which brought together historical references and contemporary media. In recognition of her outstanding contribution to art, she was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1983. Today, Anna Bella Geiger is celebrated internationally as a pioneering artist whose innovative and multidisciplinary practice has profoundly shaped the development of contemporary art in Brazil and beyond.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Fernanda Gomes (born 1960 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is a leading Brazilian contemporary artist known for her poetic and minimalist installations created from found and everyday materials. Emerging in the 1980s alongside a generation of influential Brazilian artists that includes Beatriz Milhazes, Ernesto Neto, and Adriana Varejão, Gomes developed a distinctive artistic language based on subtle interventions, accumulation, and transformation. Her work incorporates discarded objects such as old furniture, mirrors, glass, strings, newspapers, coins, magnets, cigarette ends, and other humble materials, which she carefully arranges into delicate spatial compositions. Through these installations, she explores themes of time, memory, impermanence, and the hidden beauty of ordinary objects. Rather than imposing fixed meanings, Gomes creates environments that invite contemplation and encourage viewers to become attentive to the relationships between objects, light, space, and perception. Her artistic practice is characterized by an economy of means and a refined sensitivity to material presence, often blurring the boundaries between sculpture, installation, and architecture. Since her first solo exhibition in London in 1997, she has gained international recognition through exhibitions at major museums and biennials, including the Venice Biennale, São Paulo Biennial, Istanbul Biennial, and Sydney Biennale. Her works are held in important collections such as Tate Modern, Centre Pompidou, the Vancouver Art Gallery, Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro, and Fundação Jumex. She has also created a permanent sculpture for the grounds of the Museu Serralves in Portugal, further extending her dialogue with landscape and space. Today, Fernanda Gomes is celebrated as one of the most significant voices in contemporary art, transforming ordinary materials into meditative works that reveal the poetic potential of everyday life.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Sonia Gomes (born 1948 in Caetanópolis, Minas Gerais, Brazil) is a celebrated Brazilian contemporary artist known for her expressive textile-based sculptures that transform found fabrics and everyday materials into powerful works of art. Raised in a town considered the birthplace of Brazil’s textile industry, Gomes developed an early fascination with cloth, craft, and handmade objects, often reworking clothing and creating jewelry from discarded materials as a child. Born to a Black mother and a white father, she draws deeply on her Afro-Brazilian heritage, family memories, and the traditions of popular culture, ritual, and craftsmanship that shaped her upbringing. Although she initially pursued a career in law, she made a decisive shift in 1994, enrolling at the Guignard School of Art in Belo Horizonte at the age of forty-five and beginning her professional artistic career. Her sculptures are created by twisting, knotting, sewing, stretching, and bundling textiles, giving discarded materials new life while preserving traces of their previous histories. Rather than working from predetermined plans, Gomes allows materials to guide the creative process, producing organic forms that evoke bodies, landscapes, memories, and emotional experiences. The influence of her grandmother, a healer who performed traditional blessing rituals, remains central to her understanding of art as a form of transformation, care, and spiritual connection. Her work also reflects an ongoing dialogue with Afro-Brazilian cultural traditions and artists such as Arthur Bispo do Rosário, whose legacy helped open paths for Black artists in Brazil. Internationally acclaimed, Gomes has exhibited at major museums, biennials, and galleries around the world, gaining recognition for redefining the possibilities of textile art within contemporary sculpture. Today, she is regarded as one of the most important voices in contemporary Brazilian art, celebrated for creating works that intertwine personal memory, cultural identity, and material experimentation.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Ester Grinspum (born 1955 in Recife, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist who lives and works in São Paulo. Her work occupies a space between sculpture and drawing, combining the fixed volumes of sculpture with the transience and movement of line. Rather than creating a harmonious hybrid, Grinspum explores the tension between form and line, producing works that evoke dialogue, boundaries, and spatial relationships. Her visual vocabulary, present in both her early drawings and later sculptures, emerged through a long process of refinement in which references from art history intertwine with forms of her own creation. Grinspum studied at the Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism of the University of São Paulo between 1973 and 1977 and at the Institute of Art and Decoration in São Paulo, where she studied with artists including Luiz Paulo Baravelli and Marcello Nitsche. She held her first exhibition of drawings and watercolors at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo in 1981. In 1988, she created her first sculpture, later included in the installation *O Duplo e o Tempo*, presented at the 20th São Paulo Biennial in 1989. A scholarship from the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris enabled her to study the work of Constantin Brancusi, further reinforcing her interest in continuous lines. Grinspum participated in the landmark exhibition *Como Vai Você, Geração 80?* in Rio de Janeiro in 1984, and in 2004 the Pinacoteca de São Paulo presented *Ester Grinspum: Uma Antologia*. Her works are held in major collections including the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, the Museum of Contemporary Art of the University of São Paulo, the Museum of Modern Art of São Paulo, the Brooklyn Museum, the Fonds National d`Art Contemporain, the Patricia Phelps de Cisneros Collection, and the Museo Reina Sofía.
